name: NeuralPath ClearRun Focus Regulation Implant
body_location: cranial — prefrontal cortex modulation array; subdermal processor at right temporal region
description:
The ClearRun is a focus and executive function regulation implant developed primarily for individuals with attention deficit disorders, but adopted broadly as a productivity and cognitive endurance tool across the working population. It operates through a prefrontal cortex modulation array that monitors the characteristic neural signatures of attentional drift, task-switching difficulty, and working memory interference, delivering precisely calibrated microstimulation to support sustained attention and reduce the friction of task initiation. Unlike earlier pharmaceutical approaches to ADHD management, the ClearRun is responsive rather than constant — it intensifies support during high-demand cognitive periods and withdraws to a near-passive monitoring state during rest or low-demand activity, preserving the natural rhythms of the user's cognitive life. An adaptive mode allows users to set focus 'sessions' with a duration and intensity level via the NeuralPath companion app, while an autonomous mode learns the user's work patterns over time and provides regulation support proactively. The implant does not create artificial motivation or emotional drive — it specifically addresses the regulatory layer between intention and execution.

The ClearRun's user base is enormous and heterogeneous. Its clinical core — people with diagnosed ADHD who previously managed through pharmaceuticals with variable side effects — represents only a fraction of actual installations. Students preparing for certification exams get it to survive multi-week study blocks. Gig economy workers in the Gray Zone who need to sustain concentration through 14-hour shifts get it because the alternative is stimulant abuse and burnout. Tier 3 knowledge workers get it to stay competitive in environments where everyone around them seems to be running faster. There is a version of the ClearRun story that is straightforwardly hopeful — people whose lives were genuinely limited by unregulated attention finally able to work, learn, and function with the reliability they always wanted. There is also a version that is more complicated, about a city that has structured its demands around an assumption of augmented cognition and left those who cannot or will not augment increasingly behind.
legality: Unrestricted (clinical diagnosis not required, though NeuralPath recommends consultation)
installation_requirements: Outpatient neural clinic; 90-minute procedure under local anesthetic; 30-day adaptive calibration period post-installation
maintenance: Firmware updates via NeuralPath app (automatic when in range); annual calibration check; no battery replacement — bioelectric passive draw; app subscription optional but recommended for session management

side_effects: First 2 weeks of calibration may include periods of unusual hyperfocus that are difficult to interrupt, including difficulty disengaging from low-priority tasks
Some users report a noticeable 'drop' sensation when a focus session ends — a brief flatness of motivation lasting 10-20 minutes
Mild temporal distortion during high-intensity sessions — time passing faster than expected
A minority of users report reduced spontaneous mind-wandering, which some experience as a loss of daydreaming capacity
cultural_context: The ClearRun has become one of the most culturally contested lifestyle implants in GLMZ, not because it is dangerous or unusual but because it makes visible a question the city would rather not answer directly: what is the difference between treating a disorder and optimizing a person to meet an environment's demands? Clinical advocates argue the implant is no different from glasses — a corrective tool for a real neurological variance. Critics, including a growing coalition of neurodiversity educators and labor organizers, argue that the mass adoption of focus regulation implants has allowed employers and institutions to raise cognitive endurance expectations to a level that effectively requires augmentation to meet, restructuring what counts as 'normal' performance around a tool that still costs money and requires a functioning body to host. Among users themselves, opinions vary enormously: many describe the ClearRun as the single best decision they ever made, while others quietly mourn the mental texture they feel they've traded away. The street term 'the groove' captures the experience most users report — not a dramatic transformation, but a reliable track where there used to be friction.
known_users: Students at secondary and post-secondary levels managing heavy academic loads
Adults with diagnosed ADHD transitioning away from pharmaceutical management
Gig economy and shift workers in the Gray Zone sustaining attention through long low-stimulation work periods
Tier 3 knowledge workers in data, legal, and administrative fields
Creatives who struggle with task initiation and project completion despite strong motivation
story_hooks: A gray-market firmware mod for the ClearRun promises to remove the session limits and push focus intensity beyond the safety ceiling — and it works, brilliantly, for about six weeks. The characters know someone who took it. They're starting to see the cost.

A Tier 1 school has quietly partnered with NeuralPath to offer subsidized ClearRun installations to its highest-performing students. The offer is framed as opportunity. A teacher thinks it's something else.

A character's ClearRun autonomous mode has begun initiating sessions without their input — and the sessions are directing their attention toward a very specific problem they didn't consciously decide to solve.
